note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting with fever and right earache.
The fever has been present since Monday evening (3 days duration), with a maximum recorded temperature of 38.9 °C at home.
The patient has been pulling at the right ear and was unsettled overnight.
The patient has a history of vomiting once on Tuesday, but no vomiting since.
The patient has a history of a runny nose for about a week preceding the current symptoms.
The patient has no history of a rash.
The patient has no history of chickenpox.
The patient's brother had chickenpox two weeks prior.
The patient is alert and playing this morning.
The patient's vaccinations are up to date.
The patient has been given paracetamol intermittently.
The patient's examination revealed a temperature of 38.4 °C, heart rate of 130, and breathing rate of 26.
The patient's hands and feet are warm, and the capillary refill is under two seconds.
The left tympanic membrane is normal.
The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging.
The patient's throat is mildly erythematous.
The chest examination is clear.
The diagnosis is Right acute otitis media.
There are no features of serious bacterial illness.
The plan includes regular analgesia with paracetamol 180 mg (7.5 mL of 120 mg/5 mL) up to four times daily and ibuprofen 100 mg (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL) three times daily with food.
A back-up prescription for amoxicillin 250 mg three times daily for 5 days is provided, to be collected only if the patient does not improve after three days or if symptoms worsen.
Urgent care (999 or A&E) is advised if the patient develops a non-blanching rash, becomes very drowsy or hard to wake, struggles to breathe, or stops drinking and not weeing.
Contact the GP or 111 if the fever lasts more than five days in total, if there is ear discharge, or if the patient does not improve after three days.
The patient should be reported if chickenpox develops and the patient seems very unwell.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician greeted the patient and asked if she was Poppy.
Relative identified herself as Poppy's mother, Gemma.
Clinician asked what had been happening.
Patient has had a temperature and keeps pulling at her ear.
Patient was up most of last night crying.
Relative corrected the timing of the fever duration: it was Monday evening, not Tuesday night, and lasted three days.
The patient's temperature was 38.9 °C last night on the ear thermometer.
The patient has been pulling at the right ear, mostly.
Patient reported that her ear hurts.
Patient is not eating much but is drinking okay (juice and milk).
Patient is in pants during the day and is still weeing normally, a few times today already.
Patient was sick once on Tuesday, but not since.
Patient had a runny nose for about a week before all this started.
Relative stated that the patient had no rash, and her brother had chickenpox two weeks ago.
Patient has never had chickenpox.
Patient is grumpy but herself and was playing with her brother this morning.
Patient reported no problems breathing.
Patient is healthy and all her vaccinations are up to date.
Patient takes no regular medicines and has no known drug allergies.
Patient has been given Calpol, but only when she seems really bad.
Examination findings: Temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 130, breathing rate 26, hands and feet are warm, and capillary refill is under two seconds.
Examination findings: Left eardrum is normal, the right eardrum is red and bulging, and the throat is a little red.
Examination finding: Chest is clear, and there is no rash on her skin.
Clinician suggested the condition looks like a middle ear infection on the right side, which often gets better on its own within three days.

Clinician suggested giving paracetamol 180 milligrams (7.5 mL of 120 mg/5 mL infant suspension) up to four times a day for pain, and ibuprofen 100 milligrams (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL suspension) three times a day with food.
Clinician offered a back-up prescription for amoxicillin 250 milligrams three times a day for 5 days, to be collected only if the patient does not improve after three days or if she gets worse.

Safety netting advice: Call 999 or go straight to A&E if the patient gets a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, becomes very drowsy or hard to wake, struggles to breathe, or stops drinking and not weeing.
Safety netting advice: Contact the GP or 111 if the fever lasts more than five days in total, if there is ear discharge, or if the patient does not improve after three days.
Clinician advised that chickenpox may develop in the next week or so since she has been exposed, and to let them know if she seems very unwell with it.
